Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

derivations.claim: Fix $x,x'\in S$ and write $p=k_x$, $q=k_{x'}$. The assumed ordered-pair bound gives $p\le Cq$ almost everywhere, so $q\ge p/C$. Let $A_+=\{z:p(z)\ge q(z)\}$. For every measurable $A$, $|\int_A(p-q)\,d\lambda|\le\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda$. Since $\int(p-q)=0$, the positive and negative parts have equal integral, and $\int(p-q)^+\,d\lambda=1-\int\min(p,q)\,d\lambda$; equality is attained at $A_+$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

derivations.claim: For any bounded measurable $h$ and $s\ge1$, [F1] gives $\pi_{s-1}(E_sh)=\pi_{s-1}(k_s(\upsilon_sh))=\widetilde\pi_s(\upsilon_sh)=\pi_s(h).$ Iterating this identity yields $\pi_k(E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi)=\pi_t(\bar\phi)=0$ for every $k<t$; for $k=t$ the identity operator also gives mean zero.

derivations.claim: At time $0$, [F2] and the finite particle law [F7] give IID proposal particles with law $\widetilde\pi_0$. there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$

$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. On the remaining event every proposal particle avoids proposal-null sets almost surely: initially particles have the proposal law, and inductively positive-weight selection avoids target-null sets, after which mutation avoids $\widetilde\pi_s$-null sets since $\widetilde\pi_s=\pi_{s-1}k_s$. Thus all sampled $u$ values equal one almost surely there, so residual selection is deterministic. The resampling fluctuation is zero outside an event of probability tending to zero, proving the constant-weight branch. In the other case, for the three tests $a=1,\phi,\phi^2$, where $\pi_t(\phi^2)<\infty$, one has $\frac1N\sum_i b_i^Na(X_t^i)\xrightarrow{P}\widetilde\pi_t(r(u)a).$ To verify this triangular empirical limit, fix $M$ and first restrict to $u\le M$ and $|\phi|\le M$. The compact $u$ interval meets only finitely many positive-integer discontinuities of $r$. Delete open $\gamma$-neighborhoods of those integers. On the remaining compact set, $r(u/\bar u_N)\to r(u)$ uniformly as $\bar u_N\to1$, and $|a|\le \max(1,M,M^2)$, so [F3] gives convergence of the restricted averages. [F3] controls its empirical average for each fixed $\gamma$. Taking $a=1$ in step 1.1 gives $N^{-1}\sum_i b_i^N\to c$. Thus the number $M_N=\sum_i b_i^N$ of residual draws diverges and $M_N/N\to c$. Their conditional sampling probabilities are $b_i^N/M_N$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite horizon $T$. At each $0\le t\le T$, let $\pi_t$ be a probability law on a measurable particle space $\Theta_t$. Let $\widetilde\pi_0$ be an initial proposal with $\pi_0\ll\widetilde\pi_0$, and fix $\upsilon_0=d\pi_0/d\widetilde\pi_0$. For $1\le t\le T$, let $k_t$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta_{t-1}$ to $\Theta_t$, and put
$$\widetilde\pi_t(A)=\int_{\Theta_{t-1}}k_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
Assume $\pi_t\ll\widetilde\pi_t$ and fix a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym version $\upsilon_t=d\pi_t/d\widetilde\pi_t$, so $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t)=1$. The BCS-41 sequential importance-resampling algorithm [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] is this scheme on path spaces when $k_t$ appends a proposal transition. Under the support and measurable versions of [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]], its normalized incremental weight is $\upsilon_t=(Z_{t-1}/Z_t)G_t r_t$ for $t\ge1$, and $\upsilon_0=G_0\rho_0/Z_0$ initially. The previous normalized target is already part of $\widetilde\pi_t$; one does not multiply by the full earlier path-weight product again.

For a measurable vector function $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R^d$, write $\mu(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\phi)=\int(\phi-\mu(\phi))(\phi-\mu(\phi))^\top\,d\mu,$$
when the second moment is finite. Also write $k_t\phi(x)=\int\phi(z)k_t(x,dz)$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)=\int(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))(\phi(z)-k_t\phi(x))^\top k_t(x,dz).$$

The source recursive test classes are
$$\Phi_0^{(d)}=\{\phi:\widetilde\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty\},$$
and, for $t\ge1$,
$$\Phi_t^{(d)}=\left\{\phi:\text{ for some }\delta>0,\ \widetilde\pi_t(\|\upsilon_t\phi\|^{2+\delta})<\infty\ \text{ and }\ x\mapsto k_t(\upsilon_t\phi)(x)\in\Phi_{t-1}^{(d)}\right\}.$$
Assume $1\in\Phi_t^{(1)}$ for every $t$. This is the source theorem's explicit normalizing-weight condition. For the recursive post-resampling CLTs proved on this page, use the stronger classes $\Psi_t^{(d)}$. At $t=0$, let $\Psi_0^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_0^{(d)}$ for which $\widetilde\pi_0(\|\upsilon_0(\phi-\pi_0(\phi))\|^2)<\infty$ and $\pi_0(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$. The initial normalizing denominator needs only its finite first moment $\widetilde\pi_0(\upsilon_0)=1$. For $t\ge1$, let $\Psi_t^{(d)}$ consist of the $\phi\in\Phi_t^{(d)}$ for which $\pi_t(\|\phi\|^2)<\infty$ and $x\mapsto E_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))(x)\in\Psi_{t-1}^{(d)}$. Here $E_t h=k_t(\upsilon_t h)$ is the operator defined below. Only target second moments are required: fixed-tail truncation supplies the conditional selection Lindeberg condition without a target higher-moment assumption. The recursive target moments supply the offspring variance at every earlier selection used in the induction. The source $\Phi_t$ conditions alone need not imply them. The source condition $1\in\Phi_t$ and these recursive target moments are the stated hypotheses for the CLT induction; no higher initial normalizer moment is required.

Define the mutation covariance operators recursively. At time zero,
$$\widetilde V_0(\phi)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\widetilde\pi_0}(\phi).$$
For $t\ge1$,
$$\widetilde V_t(\phi)=\widehat V_{t-1}(k_t\phi)+\int\operatorname{Cov}_{k_t}(\phi)(x)\,\pi_{t-1}(dx).$$
The weighted-estimator covariance is
$$V_t(\phi)=\widetilde V_t\!\left(\upsilon_t(\phi-\pi_t(\phi))\right).$$
For a measurable vector function $h$ on $\Theta_t$, define the forward operator from $\Theta_{t-1}$ by
$$E_t h(x)=k_t(\upsilon_t h)(x)=\int\upsilon_t(z)h(z)\,k_t(x,dz).$$
For $k<t$, write $E_{k+1:t}=E_{k+1}\circ\cdots\circ E_t$; set $E_{t+1:t}$ to the identity operator.
For multinomial offspring resampling set
$$\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{multi}}(\phi)=V_t(\phi)+\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_t}(\phi).$$
For residual offspring resampling, let $r(u)=u-\lfloor u\rfloor$. When $c_t=\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t))>0$, define the formal source candidate
$$R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}(\phi)=\widetilde\pi_t\!\left(r(\upsilon_t)\phi\phi^\top\right)-\frac{\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)\,\widetilde\pi_t(r(\upsilon_t)\phi)^\top}{c_t}.$$
Set $R_t=R_t^{\mathrm{cand}}$ and $\widehat V_t^{\mathrm{res}}=V_t+R_t$ only when $\widetilde\pi_t(\upsilon_t\in\{1,2,\ldots\})=0$; then $c_t>0$ and the finite-sample floor discontinuities are avoided. If $\upsilon_t=1$ $\widetilde\pi_t$-almost everywhere, put $R_t=0$. Residual offspring are deterministic whenever all sampled weights equal one. In SIR this holds almost surely outside earlier zero-weight fallback events, whose probability tends to zero at a fixed horizon; the almost-everywhere condition alone does not prescribe weights on proposal-null states reached after a fallback. No residual covariance is assigned when $c_t=0$ but $\upsilon_t$ is not almost everywhere one: the finite-sample normalization can move positive integer weights across floor boundaries. The B-page counterexamples show why the general positive-integer-atom branch remains unassigned.

Use the operators and multinomial variance recursion of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] at every selection time. For $\phi\in\Psi_t^{(d)}$, put $\bar\phi=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$. Then
$$V_t(\phi)=\sum_{k=0}^{t}\widetilde\pi_k\!\left[\upsilon_k^2\,E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)E_{k+1:t}(\bar\phi)^\top\right],$$
where the $k=t$ term uses $E_{t+1:t}\bar\phi=\bar\phi$. Each summand is a finite positive-semidefinite matrix under the stated class conditions.

Let $E_s$ be the forward operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]], and for bounded real $h$ put $\operatorname{osc}(h)=\sup h-\inf h$. Suppose there is one $\beta\in[0,1)$ such that
$$\operatorname{osc}(E_s h)\le\beta\operatorname{osc}(h)$$
for every $s$ and every bounded real $h$ with $\pi_s(h)=0$, with bounded measurable versions of $E_sh$. The stronger condition on every bounded $h$ is sufficient but is not necessary here. For bounded $\phi:\Theta_t\to\mathbb R$, put $\Delta\phi=\operatorname{osc}(\phi)$ and $\bar\phi=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$. Then for every $0\le k\le t$,
$$\bigl\lVert E_{k+1:t}\bar\phi\bigr\rVert_\infty\le\beta^{t-k}\Delta\phi,$$
with $\beta^0=1$ and $E_{t+1:t}$ the identity. This condition concerns the actual SMC backward operators; it is not implied merely by mixing ratios of the proposal densities.

Let $\mathsf X$ be a nonempty standard-Borel space with a sigma-finite reference measure $\lambda$, and let $\eta_0$ be a probability on it. For $s\ge1$, supply jointly measurable, strictly positive finite densities $g_s(z\mid x)$ of probability transition kernels relative to $\lambda$, and measurable likelihood factors $f_s$ with $0<a\le f_s(z)\le b<\infty$. These specified versions satisfy, for one $C\ge1$ and every $s,x,x',z$,
$$g_s(z\mid x)\le Cg_s(z\mid x').$$
Define $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)$, $\eta_s(h)=\eta_{s-1}(g_s(f_sh))/c_s$, and $E_sh(x)=g_s(f_sh)(x)/c_s$. They are the operators of [[def-smc-clt-function-classes-and-variance-recursions]] restricted to last-state tests in the corresponding filtering model. Put $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. For every bounded measurable real terminal test $\psi$ and $0\le k<t$,
$$\|E_{k+1:t}(\psi-\eta_t\psi)\|_\infty\le C\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi).$$
For $k=t$ the identity image is bounded by $\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; use $\rho^n=0$ for $n\ge1$ when $C=1$. This is a closed last-state-test assertion, not a contraction of arbitrary functions of the full stored path. Positivity, finiteness and the ratio bounds refer to the supplied pointwise density versions, not to unspecified unrelated null-set versions.

derivations.claim: Put $h_t=\phi-\pi_t(\phi)$ and $h_k=E_{k+1:t}h_t$ for $0\le k<t$, with $h_t$ itself at $k=t$. The multistep hypothesis supplies bounded versions of these centered images. By [F1], $\pi_k(h_k)=0$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}$ for $1\le k\le t$. At $k=0$, boundedness and $\upsilon_0\le B$ almost everywhere give $h_0\in\Psi_0$. If $h_{k-1}\in\Psi_{k-1}$, then boundedness of $h_k$ and $\upsilon_k\le B$ almost everywhere give $\widetilde\pi_k(|\upsilon_k h_k|^{2+\delta})<\infty$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}\in\Phi_{k-1}$, so $h_k\in\Phi_k$. Also $\pi_k(h_k^2)<\infty$ and $E_kh_k=h_{k-1}\in\Psi_{k-1}$, hence $h_k\in\Psi_k$. Induction gives $h_t\in\Psi_t$, so [F2] applies to $V_t(h_t)=V_t(\phi)$. Its summands are nonnegative and finite because $\upsilon_k\le B$ almost everywhere and each $h_k$ has a bounded version.

The multistep bound in the Statement makes the $k$th summand at most $B^2A^2\rho^{2(t-k)}(\Delta\phi)^2$. Summing the geometric series gives $V_t(\phi)\le A^2B^2(\Delta\phi)^2/(1-\rho^2)$. Applying [F3] yields the original one-step specialization.

In the filtering branch, the actual increment is $\upsilon_s(x,z)=g_s(z\mid x)f_s(z)/(c_sq_s(z\mid x))$, with $c_s=\eta_{s-1}(g_sf_s)\in[a,b]$. Hence $\upsilon_s\le Db/a$ for $s\ge1$; the initial bound gives $\upsilon_s\le B$ at every time. The last-state subspace is preserved by the filtering operators, and [F4] supplies its centered-image estimate with $A=C$, $\rho=1-C^{-2}$. Step 2.1 proves the displayed filtering bound; when $C=1$, all earlier images vanish and the same formula applies.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty measurable source space. Suppose a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on $E$ and probability densities $k_x$ satisfy $K(x,A)=\int_A k_x\,d\lambda$ for every $x\in S$ and measurable $A\subseteq E$. If $C\ge1$ and, for every $x,x'\in S$, $k_x(z)\le Ck_{x'}(z)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $z$, then the Dobrushin coefficient from [[def-dobrushin-coefficient-for-probability-kernels]] obeys
$$\delta(K)\le1-C^{-1}.$$

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces with $S\ne\varnothing$, and let $K:S\rightsquigarrow E$ be a probability kernel as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Its **Dobrushin contraction coefficient** is
$$\delta(K):=\sup_{x,x'\in S}\lVert K(x,\cdot)-K(x',\cdot)\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},$$
where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the event-supremum distance between probability laws in [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. Thus $0\le\delta(K)\le1$. The coefficient measures the largest total-variation separation between two one-step output laws.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $k<t$. Define $Q_{j,t}h(x)$ by iterating the kernels $g_{j+1},\ldots,g_t$, multiplying by $f_{j+1},\ldots,f_t$, and evaluating $h$ at the final state. Put $H_{j,t}=Q_{j,t}1$ and $H_{t,t}=1$. Measurability follows from [F1], while probability normalization and the bounds on $f_s$ give $a^{t-j}\le H_{j,t}\le b^{t-j}$. Comparing the first transition row gives $H_{j,t}(x)\le C H_{j,t}(x')$ for $j<t$. Consequently $r_{k,t}:=H_{k,t}/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ is positive, at most $C$, and has $\eta_k$-mean one.

For $j=k+1,\ldots,t$, set $L_{j,t}(x,dz)=g_j(z\mid x)f_j(z)H_{j,t}(z)\lambda(dz)/H_{j-1,t}(x)$. The recursion for $H$ shows that these are probability kernels, with strictly positive finite denominators. The ratio of two of their density rows is $[g_j(z\mid x)/g_j(z\mid x')][H_{j-1,t}(x')/H_{j-1,t}(x)]\le C^2$ by step 1.1. Thus [F3] gives $\delta(L_{j,t})\le1-C^{-2}=\rho$. Telescoping the $H$ factors in the product kernel $P_{k,t}=L_{k+1,t}\cdots L_{t,t}$ gives $P_{k,t}h=Q_{k,t}h/H_{k,t}$.

For any probability kernel $K$ and bounded real $h$ of positive oscillation, put $u=(h-\inf h)/\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Then $0\le u\le1$, and [F5] under each output law gives $K u(x)-K u(x')=\int_0^1[K(x,\{u>r\})-K(x',\{u>r\})]dr$. By [F4], its absolute value is at most $\delta(K)$. If the oscillation is zero, $K$ preserves the constant and the same oscillation bound is immediate. Hence $\operatorname{osc}(Kh)\le\delta(K)\operatorname{osc}(h)$. Iterating this inequality along the kernels in step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{osc}(P_{k,t}h)\le\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(h)$.

The filtering recursion and iterated integration [F2] yield $\eta_t h=\eta_k(Q_{k,t}h)/\eta_k(H_{k,t})$ and $\prod_{j=k+1}^tc_j=\eta_k(H_{k,t})$. Thus $E_{k+1:t}h=r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h$. Take $h=\psi-\eta_t\psi$. Then $\eta_k(r_{k,t}P_{k,t}h)=0$, and $r_{k,t}\eta_k$ is a probability by step 1.1. Therefore the global infimum of $P_{k,t}h$ is at most zero and its supremum is at least zero, so its sup norm is at most its oscillation. Step 3.1 bounds this by $\rho^{t-k}\operatorname{osc}(\psi)$; multiplying by $r_{k,t}\le C$ proves the claim. For $k=t$, the mean $\eta_t\psi$ lies between $\inf\psi$ and $\sup\psi$, giving the identity-case bound.
